narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction toward passing. However, your first-year law school grades ranked a close second and pushed strongly toward failure. These early grades placed you in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of sixth decile among students who were accepted. Your family income bracket came third; being in the upper-middle category also nudged the outcome slightly toward failure, though its effect was smaller.

Taken together, the model saw your solid LSAT performance outweighed by weaker performance in your first year of law school. The combination produced a borderline prediction that ultimately led to rejection.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Improving your grades in the remaining years, seeking additional bar-prep support, or retaking the LSAT if possible could meaningfully shift your profile for future applications. Consider speaking with an admissions counselor about how targeted improvements in these areas are viewed by law schools.
